items.title: Some North Korean workers sent to Russia are helping Ukraine war effort, report says - NBC News
items.summary: Some North Korean workers sent to Russia are helping Ukraine war effort, report says  NBC News
items.content:
A Russian network of brokers sponsored by Pyongyang has taken North Koreans to work in Russia in exploitative conditions, a rights group said. Alexander Khitrov / AP
SEOUL, South Korea — A Russian network of brokers sponsored by Pyongyang has taken North Koreans to work in Russia in exploitative conditions and in violation of U.N. sanctions, some at factories that turn out items Moscow uses in the Ukraine war , a rights group said.
The neighbors have greatly strengthened military and political ties since pledging renewed cooperation at a 2023 summit of their leaders, while a mutual defense pact is a cornerstone of a partnership treaty signed the following year.
In its report , the Hague-based group, Global Rights Compliance (GRC), said North Korea reaps funds from the operation, taking much of the wages earned by its workers who are sent to Russia and made to stay under threat of retribution.
The group cites open-source information on the operation run by a Russian businessman, facial recognition technology to identify North Korean officials, and evidence gathered by its members posing undercover as prospective employers.
“This investigation exposes a dangerous convergence between two states’ military ambitions,” said the group’s legal adviser, Elise Lauriot Prevost.
These were “North Korea’s use of overseas forced labor to finance its weapons program, and Russia’s growing reliance on labor to sustain its war economy,” she added.
Russia’s foreign ministry and the North Korean Embassy in Moscow did not respond to emails seeking comment.
The rights group said it contacted two Russians identified as key figures in the network, but only one replied, denying the accusation. It did not say whether the other responded.
Since 2024, North Korea has sent more than 10,000 troops to fight alongside Russians in the Ukraine war, as well as weapons to replenish Moscow’s dwindling armory while gaining valuable battlefield experience, South Korea’s intelligence agency has said.
To evade U.N. sanctions that ban member nations from hiring North Korean workers, the latter enter Russia on student visas in the guise of enrolling at colleges, GRC said.
Then they are contracted out to Russian employers, with brokers receiving a commission of up to 150,000 rubles ($1,860) for each, it added.
GRC investigators posed undercover as prospective employers and found the workers were hired at production sites, including a military rations factory.
The workers are forced to stay on the job through coercion and threats of retribution against them and their families.
One advertisement assured prospective employers that workers would not “run away,” the report said. Workers labor 12-hour days with two days off each month, it added, citing such ads.
After North Korea’s sixth and last nuclear test in 2017, a U.N. Security Council resolution put a blanket ban on the hiring of its workers overseas and mandated their return home.
Russia and China , two permanent members of the Security Council that voted for the ban, have since been accused by South Korea and the West of noncompliance with resolutions.
Such measures, dating back to 2006, banned the flow of goods, energy, weapons and workers with North Korea.
In previous years, Russia employed North Korean laborers in its far east while many North Koreans staffing restaurants in China sent home wages that were channeled to the state treasury, rights groups have said.
North Korea is directly involved in running the network supplying workers in Russia, with officials from its Moscow embassy identified as inspecting work sites for prospective employment, the GRC report said.
“These workers do not come cheap, yet little, if any, of the money paid for their labor reaches them,” said Dylan Carter, a GRC lead investigator.
“Instead, it lines the pockets of the DPRK state,” he added, referring to North Korea by a short version of its official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

items.title: Federal Reserve leaves interest rates unchanged despite rising inflation - NBC News
items.summary: Federal Reserve leaves interest rates unchanged despite rising inflation  NBC News
items.content:
Federal Reserve keeps interest rates unchanged in final vote before midterms
Oct. 28, 2026, 2:01 PM EDT  /  Updated   Oct. 28, 2026, 2:44 PM EDT
The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep interest rates unchanged, its final monetary policy decision before the midterm elections.
The decision to hold rates steady came despite inflation that jumped from a 3.4% annual rate in August to 3.7% in September .
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also announced that the central bank will reduce the number of meetings at which it votes on interest rates from eight to seven next year and by two in 2028. Warsh said that the seismic change to the schedule would help improve the “quality” of its decisions.
A major driver of that inflation is the soaring cost of gas, diesel and crude oil. These higher prices have hit consumers hard, and many economists say the spillover effect of rising gas prices has started to show up across the broader economy.
In its post-decision statement, the Fed acknowledged the problem that inflation is causing but said it needs more data before moving forward with a rate hike.
“Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal,” it said.
The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, will not be released until Thursday; it is expected to touch 3.7%.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh after a Federal Open Market Committee meeting Wednesday. Al Drago / Bloomberg via Getty “This suggests that the Fed might not be done tightening and future hikes will depend on the incoming data,” economists at Morgan Stanley said. In central bank speak, “tightening” refers to raising rates.
“As we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction,” Warsh said in a post-meeting news conference. “That’s good news, but inflation is too high.”
“Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy,” he added.

Wednesday’s vote was not unanimous, unlike September’s 12-0 vote to hike rates , the first time since 2023 that the central bank had raised its benchmark rate.
Two officials, governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of a rate hike. The dissent by Cook, whom President Donald Trump is attempting to fire, was her first ever.
An interest rate hike could have added slightly more pressure to already beleaguered consumers.
Voters have consistently told pollsters that rising prices, especially in the housing and energy sectors, are their primary concerns as they cast their ballots.
The most recent NBC News poll found Trump’s approval rating at 27% for his handling of the cost of living and 29% for his handling of the Iran war.
Two-thirds of Americans said the soaring gas prices triggered by Trump’s Iran war were either a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem. More than half of respondents said current economic conditions had caused them to change what kinds of groceries they buy.
Warsh said the midterms and politics “played no role in the decision” to keep rates where they are.
Asked about Trump’s recent claims that members of the Fed’s board and rate-setting committee were hostile to the president, Warsh defended his colleagues.
“We just came out of a heck of a family fight, serious, sober discussion,” he said. “I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment, and I’m honored to be here and honored to be the chairman of this group.”
The central bank also acknowledged the economic anxiety gripping much of the country.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”
Wednesday’s announcement and the Fed’s acknowledgment that inflation remains well above its goal set the stage for a rate increase during December’s monetary policy meeting.

items.title: Microsoft Maia 300: Could Its New AI Chip Challenge NVIDIA? - Cloud Wars
items.summary: Microsoft Maia 300: Could Its New AI Chip Challenge NVIDIA?  Cloud Wars
items.content:
In today’s Cloud Wars Minute, I analyze Microsoft’s ambitious Maia 300 rollout and how owning its own AI chips could give the company greater control over its AI infrastructure, improve efficiency, and reduce its reliance on NVIDIA.
00:10 — Microsoft has announced Maia 300 , the company's latest custom AI chip. It's also revealed plans to expand its Azure Maia systems to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, and with this rollout, Maia will become the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services.
01:02 — Microsoft expects Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. In other words, Microsoft expects to deliver more AI output for the same amount of power. That's crucial as demand for AI services continues to skyrocket. Now, Microsoft also says that in a full configuration, Maia 300 systems are expected to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.
01:41 — Bear in mind that Maia 200 is already a very capable system, and Maia 300 really builds on those foundations — I'm going to quote Microsoft here: "To enable more coding with GitHub, more flexible AI model deployment through Microsoft Foundry, and faster interactions with Copilot, Teams, and Dragon Copilot." Now, back to that incredibly important point I made at the start.
02:05 — Maia is set to become the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services. Now, back in August, I talked about what this could mean for NVIDIA. My conclusion was that Microsoft's own chips could help level the playing field and give the company more options.
02:33 — Could Microsoft chips potentially challenge NVIDIA in the market? I think that remains to be seen. Microsoft's announcement certainly seems to suggest that it will have more control over its AI infrastructure , but it doesn't necessarily mean that NVIDIA is being pushed out of the picture altogether. What is clear, though, is that Microsoft is moving towards a much more full-circle AI business with its own chips, cloud infrastructure, models, and applications.

items.title: What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash
items.summary: More than 500 passengers were on board the trains when the crash occurred in the province of Toledo, south of Madrid.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Aerial footage shows train crash scene
Two trains have crashed in Spain just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday morning.
Rail operator Adif says the incident occurred between a Renfe train and another of the Iryo company, which covers the Madrid to Seville route.
So far at least 68 people are confirmed to have died in the incident.
The two trains crashed just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.
The accident happened when a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to the south of the country barrelled into another train that was apparently stationary. The crash caused at least two carriages to fall down an embankment.
Broadcaster RTVE, quoting the transport ministry, said a Renfe train rear-ended an Iryo train.
Renfe is Spain's national state-owned railway company while Iryo is a private high-speed railway operator.
All train traffic on this line has been stopped at stations along the route, Adif said.
Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia remain suspended.
A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.
Image source, 1vanta3 / X via Anadolu / Getty Images
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown.
Transport minister Oscar Puente has said a computer failure led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre which decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks further ahead.
Audio recordings between train controllers in Madrid and the train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another up ahead had stalled.

items.content:
China Is Building Its Way Around Europe’s EV Tariffs
Beijing’s evolving industrial playbook is taking shape in Morocco.
By Aaron Glasserman , a distinguished fellow at the Weatherhead East Asian Institute at Columbia University and a fellow on foreign policy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, and Jessie Jiexi Lin , a student pursuing a master’s in public administration at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs.
Workers in dark uniforms and blue baseball caps inspect the metal frames of silver, unpainted electric vehicles along a brightly lit assembly line on a factory floor. The line of cars extends backward to the far wall, with similar small groups of workers bustling around each one.
Workers check vehicle frames on the production line for electric vehicle maker Zeekr at its factory in Ningbo, China, on May 29, 2025. Kevin Frayer/Getty Images
In recent years, Europe’s auto industry has reeled from the influx of low-cost, high-quality Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Even as Brussels imposes tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, their market share only continues to grow. As of December, more than 9 percent of all new automobiles sold in Europe were made in China, with some estimates expecting Chinese EVs to account for roughly 20 percent of the Western European market by 2028.
Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs reflect a common Western view that high-value Chinese products are competitive in global markets largely because of state subsidies . To be sure, China’s EV industry has benefited immensely from Beijing’s subsidies, easy credit, and tax relief. That explanation, however, is far too narrow and risks severely underestimating the scale of the challenge ahead.
In recent years, Europe’s auto industry has reeled from the influx of low-cost, high-quality Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Even as Brussels imposes tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, their market share only continues to grow. As of December, more than 9 percent of all new automobiles sold in Europe were made in China, with some estimates expecting Chinese EVs to account for roughly 20 percent of the Western European market by 2028.
Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs reflect a common Western view that high-value Chinese products are competitive in global markets largely because of state subsidies . To be sure, China’s EV industry has benefited immensely from Beijing’s subsidies, easy credit, and tax relief. That explanation, however, is far too narrow and risks severely underestimating the scale of the challenge ahead.
The more consequential story—that will likely make Chinese EVs even more competitive in the near future—is Beijing’s evolving approach to overseas industrial policy. At the core of this approach is an increasingly coordinated model of public- and private-sector activity.
State-owned enterprises (SOE) lay the groundwork for favorable investment environments abroad by undertaking massive infrastructure projects and securing access to strategic resources. Boosted by Beijing’s diplomatic ties and international clout, private companies leverage these state-backed platforms as a springboard for trade by bringing in investment, production capacity, and industry-specific expertise.
The advantages of this approach for Beijing—and the challenge that it poses to foreign companies—are already on full display in Morocco, where years of existing strategic investment, infrastructure development, and geopolitical maneuvering are pushing China closer to vertically integrating EV supply chains, bypassing tariffs, and further reshaping Europe’s auto industry.
It is only in recent years that Morocco has emerged as a key node in China’s EV empire.
For decades, Beijing maintained much closer ties with Morocco’s neighbor and rival, Algeria, but that began to change in the early 2010s as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) took off. In 2016, Morocco joined the growing ranks of countries signing “strategic partnerships” with China, making mutual commitments to expand economic cooperation and recognize each other’s core interests.
The next year, Morocco officially entered the BRI, and China has since poured millions of dollars into Morocco’s energy and transportation sectors . Almost a decade later, that economic relationship has expanded dramatically: In March, China’s committed investment in the country exceeded $10 billion , concentrated mostly in the EV and energy sectors.
China’s EV manufacturing capacity in Morocco builds on years of large-scale, state-backed investment in transportation infrastructure and natural resources. Over the past decade, Chinese SOEs have collaborated on major infrastructure and development projects in Morocco, including bridges , highways , and smart cities . Some of these are directly relevant to the EV industry, such as the chemical processing unit in Khouribga, home to one of the world’s biggest reserves of phosphate, which is critical for EV battery production .
This SOE-led scramble for resources and construction-heavy projects paved the way for private Chinese companies in the EV sector to establish footholds in Morocco and ship to overseas markets. Tanger Tech City, China’s SOE-led flagship collaboration with Morocco, is located less than 30 miles from Tanger Med, the largest container port in Africa. Taking advantage of no-fee business registration and tax-free dividends, private Chinese companies—including the global battery giant BTR New Material Group as well as tire manufacturers Sentury Tire and Guizhou Tyre—have established or announced plans to establish production bases in the industrial zone.
Elsewhere in the country, major private investments include battery manufacturer Gotion’s $1.3 billion factory and a $2 billion joint-venture battery materials factory between China’s CNGR Advanced Material and the Moroccan private equity firm Al Mada.
This isn’t to deny the role of subsidies and preferential financing, which Beijing sees as key tools for supporting companies that are expanding internationally. A 2024 directive , for instance, called on Chinese financial institutions to improve credit approval and lending procedures and to enhance cross-border settlement to “better support companies expanding into international markets.” Closer collaboration among Chinese banks, semi-official trade organizations, and Moroccan banks has also helped to streamline financing and channel investment into the African market.
But these policies are useful to Chinese firms because they are operating in an industrial landscape that SOEs have already shaped, with relatively easy access to necessary resources and infrastructure.
China’s success with this approach has only been possible because it also advances Rabat’s desire to expand domestic manufacturing capability and position Morocco as Africa’s next industrial powerhouse. Chinese investment is expected to generate sorely needed jobs; Morocco’s unemployment rate has hardly dipped below 10 percent for the past decade, and youth unemployment in cities stands at a staggering 47 percent. Officials claim that the Gotion factory alone will create 17,000 local jobs, including 2,300 high-skilled positions.
Beijing has coupled this economic engagement with a subtle diplomatic shift in favor of Rabat’s claims over Western Sahara . For decades, China has avoided explicitly backing either Morocco or Western Sahara, though its rhetoric often leaned toward the latter—and thus to the latter’s main sponsor, Algiers . With one exception in 2018, it consistently voted in favor of United Nations Security Council resolutions extending the peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara and affirming support for the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination.
However, in recent years, China has done an about-face. In 2024, its Ministry of Foreign Affairs implicitly acknowledged the importance of the Western Sahara question for Rabat, stating , “China supports Morocco in maintaining national security and stability and is ready to work with Morocco to continue firmly supporting each other on issues concerning their respective core interests.” Then, last fall, Beijing abstained on the most recent U.N. resolution on the matter, which for the first time endorsed Rabat’s proposal to formally establish Western Sahara as an autonomous region under Moroccan sovereignty.
The full payoff of China’s Moroccan gambit will materialize if and when localized EV manufacturing matures, which could take years. That is still a tall order, as evidenced by the recent shelving of a BYD assembly plant project that had been stalled since 2017 due to budget issues and limited local charging infrastructure, according to a company executive.
Though Chinese automakers are not yet building assembly plants in Morocco, the country matters for everything “upstream” of assembly. It is becoming an integrated ecosystem for the production of batteries, tires, and other components, which reduces Chinese EV companies’ reliance on direct shipments from China and lowers costs for Chinese assembly plants in Europe and Africa.
Morocco also offers Chinese firms convenient access to the European market through the Tanger Med port and—more importantly—a rules-based pathway through Brussels’s tightening trade defenses . Currently, the EU imposes duties of up to 35 percent on EVs manufactured in China. However, vehicles that qualify as Moroccan in origin can enter the European market duty-free. That includes vehicles assembled in Morocco, so long as foreign parts make up less than 45 percent of the finished vehicle’s ex-works price.
In short, if Chinese EV companies succeed in establishing vehicle assembly factories and fully integrating supply chains in Morocco, they will be able to sell vehicles to Europe under a “Made in Morocco” label, avoiding both the 10 percent EU standard automobile tariff and the additional punitive tariff on Chinese-made EVs—reducing the total tariff effect from as much as 45 percent to zero. This would pose an unprecedented threat to what remains one of the EU’s most important industries .
China is rolling out this coordinated approach to overseas industrial policy elsewhere to varying degrees.
In Thailand, for example, China is a key investor in the Eastern Economic Corridor, a flagship regional development initiative anchored by a high-speed railway that will connect several Thai cities and seaports to China. The corridor has, in turn, provided an attractive environment for private Chinese investment. China is now the corridor’s largest source of foreign direct investment, primarily in the EV sector and related industries. Like Tanger Tech City, the corridor offers private Chinese companies major tax incentives and more convenient access to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ market.
The United Arab Emirates offers another example. In 2017, Chinese SOE Jiangsu Provincial Overseas Cooperation and Investment Company Limited (JOCIC) partnered with Abu Dhabi Ports to develop an industrial and special economic zone inside the Khalifa Port’s free trade zone. JOCIC set up a wholly owned UAE subsidiary to manage the park, which lets it attract Chinese private capital while insulating the parent company from project-level and geopolitical risk. The park’s location provides Chinese companies with a convenient base for expansion into the Persian Gulf and wider Middle Eastern markets, along with exemptions from value-added tax and other financial incentives . As of 2025, more than 40 Chinese companies had collectively committed more than $700 million to the park, with a focus on EVs and renewable energy.
Beijing has long seen its SOEs as tools for advancing its broader economic interests. As China in recent years has emphasized “small and beautiful” projects , the SOE-led megaprojects are often viewed as commercially disappointing holdovers from an earlier and more profligate era of BRI. Nevertheless, under this coordinated strategy, Beijing has been able to capitalize on the advantages secured by past infrastructure projects and deepen its presence in the overseas market.
As governments in industrialized economies respond to China’s surge of high-value manufactured exports, they must recognize how the sources of Chinese firms’ advantages are changing. Today, those advantages come not just from subsidies and cheap credit at home but also from integrated ecosystems abroad, built through coordination between public and private enterprise.
This means that Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs and the recently announced limits on hybrid EVs imported from China, on their own, are unlikely to stem the tide of EVs made by Chinese firms operating around the world. China’s rivals—even in industrialized economies—will struggle to compete unless they can coordinate across borders and build supply chains and infrastructure that leverage or, far less plausibly, completely sidestep what China has already put in place.

items.title: Dharshini David: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions still unanswered
items.summary: The chancellor talked of charting a new course for Britain, but the impact of Iran war has limited his options.
items.content:
Image caption, While earnings are rising, forecasters predict that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes
John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.
It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses â and the government's ability to help.
While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.
The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.
Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.
But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.
Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%
However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by Â£14bn in the past year alone.
The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.
As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be Â£160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.
And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.
So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.
The markets seem reassured â even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.
Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.
Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas â justice and higher education for example â are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.
There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.
And issues around the other big area of spending â welfare â remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by Â£100bn.
The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further Â£13bn.
Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.
Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution â but there is much to be fleshed out.
And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.
Between regulation and higher costs â in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.
So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.
With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.
The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.
So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.
For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.
A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

Fed rate decision and Warsh news conference: 5 takeaways
Even though the interest-rate vote went as expected, there were a few surprises out of this week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
One of the two dissenting votes, from Lisa Cook, raised eyebrows.
A change by the Federal Reserve will limit the number of scheduled chances to adjust rates in future years.
Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a news conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.
The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate steady . At the press conference that followed, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh disclosed some of his thinking about where the U.S. economy stands, and how that affects monetary policy. But for Fed wonks, the big news may have been Warsh's disclosure of some procedural changes ahead.
No surprises : Markets had been widely expecting the Fed to hold, and it did just that. In explaining its decision, the Federal Open Market Committee emphasized a patient approach , saying, "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
Well, one surprise : If there was one eyebrow-raising moment from the afternoon, it was Warsh's disclosure of changes in how the FOMC will meet. In 2027, the committee will still meet eight times, but one of the meetings will not entail a vote on interest rates, or include a post-meeting statement. The "strategy" meetings will increase to two the next year, leaving just six opportunities to adjust rates — outside of emergency meetings.
OK, two surprises : The FOMC vote to hold policy where it stands was widely expected. Dissent from multiple members also came as no shock. But one of the "no" votes coming from Governor Lisa Cook was a stunner. Governors rarely dissent from rate votes, and Cook hasn't done so at all since taking her seat in 2022. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack also opposed the decision. Both likely will provide statements explaining their votes before the end of the week.
The AI impact : Warsh took the opportunity to talk about the impact artificial intelligence is having on economic growth, essentially saying that it was just one of several factors driving an expansion that he said was running strong.
More musical chairs : The September meeting featured a shortened post-meeting news conference — cut from the usual 45 minutes or so down to half an hour, about the time of Wednesday's event. Moreover, reporters have been limited to a single question, a switch from prior practices when media members would take a two-for-one approach. Finally, Warsh has changed the seating in the room, going from a largely arbitrary approach — with representatives of larger outfits up front — to alphabetical order last month. This month featured reverse alphabetical order, keeping the bearers of the microphone on their toes.

How the latest Fed decision could affect your wallet
Treasury's Bessent says ‘not necessarily’ a mistake if the Fed hikes again
"The Fed is leaning into patience. It seems they prefer to wait for more information on the appropriate level of rates, as uncertainty reigns supreme in light of recent geopolitical developments." —Phil Camporeale, chief investment strategist, JPMorgan Wealth Management.
"The Fed has time on its side ... But the direction of travel remains clear. The Fed is still taking back some of last year's rate cuts, and the two dissents underline that tightening bias. We expect a hike in December and another in early 2027." — Seema Shah, chief global strategist, Principal Asset Management .
"We hesitate to characterize his communication as particularly dovish or hawkish ... The bottom line is that the Fed policy reaction is not a black-and-white, binary thing ... The market has adjusted to Warsh's communication style, but there might be a ways to go before they are fully on the same page." — Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist, Jefferies .

European countries will not be included in the next round of talks with Ukraine and the United States planned to take place in Abu Dhabi, according to a top foreign policy aide at the Kremlin.
Interfax news agency quoted Yuri Ushakov, who said the possible participation of European countries was not discussed during a  90-minute phone call on Tuesday among Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.

Speaking at a news conference in the Netherlands on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said trilateral talks with Russia and the US would take place from November 6 to November 10 in the United Arab Emirates.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv wanted Europe to also be involved in the talks, adding that unity and stronger pressure on Russia were needed.
His comments came after he met with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who pledged an extra 500 million euros ($556m) for military support to Ukraine this winter to buy drones and other material to strengthen Ukraine’s defences. Zelenskyy is also due to meet Dutch King Willem-Alexander on Wednesday.
Earlier in the day before Zelenskyy’s visit, the Dutch government announced a new support package for Ukraine worth 1.2 billion euros ($1.33bn) over the next three years and a contribution of 40 million euros ($44.5m) by the end of this year to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund.
“Support for recovery and reconstruction can’t wait for a ceasefire. Ukraine needs our help right now – military support but also social and economic assistance,” Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation, said during a visit to Kyiv on Wednesday.
“However successful you are on the battlefield, it’s also essential that energy systems, hospitals and food production keep ticking over,” he added.
In a separate development, Zelenskyy thanked British Prime Minister Andy Burnham for a newly announced additional support package worth 10 billion pounds ($13.3bn) after a Wednesday morning phone call.
“A truly strong and very timely step – coming right as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone to deal with the problems Russia is so eager to escalate,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
According to Downing Street , the new British aid package for Ukraine includes 500 million pounds ($665m) in additional military support from the Ministry of Defence “to plug urgent gaps in Ukraine’s air defences this winter”.

U.S. stock futures are mixed early Thursday as Wall Street navigates a tech-led pullback, critical PCE inflation data, and retreating oil prices amid renewed diplomatic hopes in the Middle East. Thursday follows the Federal Reserve decision to hold the benchmark interest rate steady at 3.75%-4% on Wednesday.
The Polymarket traders, a Polygon (CRYPTO: POL) based prediction platform, are leaning slightly bearish for the Oct. 29 trading session. The "S&P 500 (SPX) Up or Down on October 29?" contract currently reflects a 47% chance of a higher open.
Traders are balancing steep drops in tech futures against a favorable macroeconomic data slate and cooling energy costs:
Divergent Index Futures: A tech selloff is dragging the broader market lower, while small caps and blue chips advance. Nasdaq 100 futures dropped 1.14%, and S&P 500 futures fell 0.32%. Conversely, Russell 2000 futures gained 0.62%, and Dow Jones futures rose 0.44%.
Geopolitics & Retreating Oil: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi signaled that Tehran is giving diplomacy "a chance to succeed" and remains in contact with intermediaries to review a seven-day plan to de-escalate tensions. Energy markets retreated on the news; Brent crude slipped 1.37% to $110.11 a barrel, while WTI crude dropped 1.50% to $101.24 a barrel.
Earnings & Eco Data: Thursday's crucial economic docket features the third-quarter advance GDP, September's PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, and initial jobless claims at 8:30 a.m. ET. The corporate calendar is headlined by earnings from Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ: AMZN ), Eli Lilly & Co. (NYSE: LLY ), Mastercard Inc. (NYSE: MA ), Intel Corp. (NASDAQ: INTC ), Merck & Co. Inc. (NYSE: MRK ), and Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE: CAT ).
Market analyst Louis Navellier highlighted a surge in consumer optimism, with the Conference Board's consumer confidence index jumping to 91.7 in October from 84.2 in September. The rebound in consumer confidence offers a potentially encouraging signal heading into the holiday shopping season, although consumers continue to cite elevated costs.
Despite the pre-market weakness in tech futures, Navellier remains highly bullish on AI infrastructure stocks, pointing to massive fundamental earnings beats. GE Vernova Inc. (NYSE: GEV ) reported a 96% surge in Q3 new orders to $29 billion, while Vertiv Holdings Co. (NYSE: VRT ) saw sales jump 60.8% alongside a 91.2% earnings spike.
Navellier argues that fundamentally superior data center stocks will continue to bounce back from any short-term, sentiment-driven pullbacks and resume their upward trajectory.
The Oct. 28 Polymarket contract successfully resolved "Up". The contract recorded $33,567 in total trading volume.

U.S. Natural Gas Production Hits New Records as Demand Surges
U.S. natural gas production is set to hit consecutive records, reaching 112.2 Bcf/d in 2026 and a projected 116.1 Bcf/d in 2027.
Soaring LNG exports and AI data center demand are driving production growth, particularly in the Permian and Haynesville basins.
Producers are consolidating to capitalize on rising demand, highlighted by EQT's acquisition of Range Resources, while stronger output could push Henry Hub prices lower in 2027.
U.S. natural gas production is on track to close a second consecutive year with record-high natural gas output as producers respond to demand signs both at home and overseas.
Soaring demand for powering data centers in the United States and rising liquefied natural gas exports amid expanding liquefaction capacity, as well as surging global demand for spot LNG cargoes in the absence of Qatar’s gas due to the Iran war, are pushing American natural gas production higher this year.
Output is on track to beat in 2026 the record set in 2025 as more associated gas is being produced in the Permian basin along with oil, and operators boost gas output in the Haynesville basin, which is close to LNG export terminals and major domestic industrial gas users, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) says .
Rising production will more than offset higher LNG exports, resulting in an average Henry Hub spot price for natural gas of $3.16 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) in 2027, down by 9% compared to 2026, the EIA’s latest Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) showed earlier this month.
For this year, U.S. dry natural gas production is set to jump to 112.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) from 107.64 bcfd last year. In 2027, U.S. natural gas production is forecast to further grow to 116.13 bcfd to another record high, the EIA’s latest monthly estimates showed . Related: UBS Sees $110 Brent by Year-End as Gulf Flows Stay Below Prewar Levels
U.S. LNG exports averaged 17.4 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) in the first six months of the year, 23% higher compared to the same period in 2025, as export capacity jumped and boosted shipments to the fastest pace since exports began a decade ago.
In the domestic market, data centers have turned to additional gas-fired power generation to support the booming AI market.
Amid rising gas demand, both in the U.S. and overseas, American gas producers are raising production and entering in strategic transactions to scale and expand.
Just this week, EQT Corporation and Range Resources announced a definitive merger agreement, under which EQT will buy Range in an all-stock transaction that will create America’s leading natural gas company with a pro-forma enterprise value over $50 billion.
“North American gas markets have shifted from producer-push to demand-pull, and this deal puts EQT firmly at the heart of that transition,” said Lydia Walker, Senior Research Analyst on Wood Mackenzie’s Lower 48 upstream team.
“Range cements EQT's position as the supplier of choice for Appalachian power generation and data centre growth, adding the scale, inventory and liquids diversification needed to serve that demand for decades to come,” Walker added.
A day later, EQT raised its 2026 production guidance by about 90 Bcfe, due to better-than-expected benefits from compression investments improving both existing and new wells and shallowing decline rates, while it reduced its full-year capital spending guidance by $25 million.
Thanks to “strong performance to date”, EQT also raised its full-year 2026 total sales volume guidance to 2,375 – 2,450 Bcfe.
Meanwhile, Range Resources raised its third-quarter natural gas production by 11% from a year earlier, and year-to-date output by 5% compared to January-September 2025.
“We have considerable momentum across our business and will be exiting 2026 in the strongest position in Range’s history,” CEO Dennis Degner said.
“With EQT, we will have improved market access, best-in-class inventory, enhanced cash flow generation, and fortified resiliency to drive profitable growth and shareholder value creation through commodity cycles.”
Expand Energy, currently the largest U.S. natural gas producer before the EQT-Range deal is completed early next year, said this week in the Q3 earnings release that it is positioning itself for a “historic wave of structural domestic demand growth” underway.
“A new era of demand-pull replaces historical supply-push dynamics across the U.S.,” Expand Energy said.

The United States Federal Reserve is set to hold interest rates steady in its final monetary policy decision before the US midterm elections.
The central bank will maintain rates at 3.75-4 percent, following a 10-2 vote, in line with expectations.

CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, indicated that there was more than a 90 percent chance rates would remain unchanged.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the Fed said in its press release announcing the decision on Wednesday. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”
It also added, “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”
The most recent Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed the annual inflation rate increasing to 3.7 percent in September , up from 3.4 percent in August, with energy prices largely accounting for the monthly surge.
There were signs earlier this month that the central bank would maintain benchmark interest rates, with the Fed’s chair for supervision, Michelle Bowman, advocating a “wait and see” approach.
“I don’t feel any urgency for taking further action at this point,” she said at this month’s International Monetary Fund-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. “We really need to take some time and understand how things will evolve.”
The decision comes before Thursday’s release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index report, which is used by the central bank to assess inflation and inform its decisions.
Today’s Fed announcement follows an interest-rate hike rise last month, amid surging inflation – the first increase by the central bank since July 2023. The move drew criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pressed the Fed to cut rates since taking office. At the time, he wrote on Truth Social that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”
The Fed’s next monetary policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9, when it will give its final rate decision of the year.
Current forecasts point to a quarter-point interest rate increase.

Treasury yields tick higher after Fed interest rate decision
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., August 4, 2026.
Bond yields moved higher on Wednesday as investors digested the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady at its October meeting.
The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 3 basis points higher at 5.026%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, slipped more than 3 basis points to 4.704%.
The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was also up by more than 4 basis points to 5.354%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said the bank remained focused on "price stability" despite the pause and that the employment picture has been "quite positive."
Despite the hold for October, expectations for a 25 basis points hike at the central bank's next meeting on Dec. 9 currently stand at 85.7%, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
More economic data is due Thursday. Personal consumption expenditures index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — as well as the quarterly GDP growth rate and personal income and spending data will offer investors additional insights into the domestic economy and inflation picture.
That data will be critical to determining where the Fed may go from here, according to TruStage chief economist Steve Rick.
"Holding rates steady doesn't necessarily mean the Fed is finished raising them, especially if inflation doesn't start to cool," he said. "Policymakers will want to see whether these price pressures are temporary or becoming more widespread throughout the economy."

items.content:
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, and the chancellor, John Healey, during a visit last week to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire. Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/Treasury
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, and the chancellor, John Healey, during a visit last week to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire. Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/Treasury
Angry Labour MPs urge leadership not to overrule energy secretary on Rosebank
Exclusive: Backbenchers voice alarm over ‘intolerable position’ faced by Miatta Fahnbulleh over oilfield decision
Furious Labour MPs have been lobbying the prime minister and chancellor not to overrule the energy secretary should she decide to block the Rosebank oilfield.
MPs say they are alarmed at the cabinet splits that have emerged over the issue after sources told the Guardian that Miatta Fahnbulleh was minded to refuse environmental permission for the field.
Sources close to the chancellor, John Healey, have since made it clear he is in favour of the scheme, while some in government believe the prime minister, Andy Burnham , also wants it to go ahead.
Backbenchers worried about the environmental impact of the project are now urging their whips and Downing Street not to allow other ministers to intervene in Fahnbulleh’s decision.
Catherine Fookes, a Labour member of the energy select committee, said: “Approving Rosebank will blow a hole in our green credentials. A group of us is making it clear to leadership that this should be Miatta’s decision and I hope they listen.
Climate damage would obliterate any economic benefits of new North Sea fields, analysis shows
“Labour MPs are really, really concerned about it – it would go against the thrust of our manifesto.”
Another MP said: “If Healey pushes through Rosebank, there will be blood. It’s economically shortsighted as well as politically explosive – they aren’t listening at all to the discomfort on the backbenches.”
Another commented: “Lots of us have raised this. I think the position Miatta has been put in by these briefings is intolerable.” Concerns are understood to also have been raised with Healey directly in budget meetings with MPs.
Fahnbulleh’s parliamentary aides have circulated a memo to MPs insisting she would have the final say on the proposals, after a number of MPs contacted them to raise concerns that she would be overruled.
“No decision has been made on Rosebank,” the memo said. “The energy secretary will consider all relevant factors in a case before reaching a decision.
“The energy secretary is the only decision maker and will consider all relevant factors as part of the quasi-judicial process. No other cabinet member or minister has any role in this decision and does not see the advice on it,” it added.
Map showing location of Rosebank oilfield Burnham has promised to take a “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil drilling, calling the Jackdaw gasfield, which the government approved last week, “a bridge to the future”.
The prime minister insists the decision over Rosebank will be for Fahnbulleh alone to make.
But he prompted speculation about his support for the project on Wednesday, when he told the Commons: “Use of our reserves can support and accelerate a clean energy future, and that was very much the logic behind the decision that the government announced on Jackdaw last week.”
Many in government believe Fahnbulleh can approve the bigger Rosebank scheme without breaching the UK’s carbon commitments, in part because most of its oil would be exported.
The Guardian also revealed on Tuesday that the Treasury had already factored in tax revenues from the scheme, which are expected to hit about £500m by the end of this parliament.
Treasury officials said on Wednesday the money had been included in forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) since 2019, and that doing so would not prevent the energy secretary from blocking it.
The OBR said in its budget forecast on Wednesday: “The projection includes production from currently producing fields (including Jackdaw), and the North Sea Transition Authority’s estimate of production from development of new fields, which includes Rosebank, and from future discoveries.
“The forecast annual pace of decline [in oil and gas production] would be around 14% a year if there were no production from any new fields.”
The memo from Fahnbulleh’s aides added that decisions to score Rosebank as part of the forecast would be a decision for the OBR.
Burnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaigners
However, some Labour MPs believe the Treasury has been using aggressive tactics to strong-arm the energy department, with one describing the approach of No 11 as “macho bullshit”.
Clive Lewis, another Labour MP, said: “You cannot claim global climate leadership while approving new oilfields simply because you’ve already pencilled in the tax receipts. Tax ‘receipts’, as I understand it, that will be the operator’s estimate and not actual Treasury revenue.”
Analysis by Uplift, a campaign group, found that on the government’s and industry’s estimates, the tax take from Rosebank would probably be limited and could be outweighed by the tax breaks and incentives likely to be offered for the development and decommissioning of the fields.
Areeba Hamid, a co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said: “Any tax revenues from this far-off field in a rapidly declining basin don’t just leave our public services at the hostage of future oil prices, they also leave taxpayers on the hook for the costs of decommissioning for decades to come. The truth is that approving new oil drilling in the North Sea will only add to the costs of climate impacts, costs not fully factored into forecasts such as those from the OBR. Any economist should be able to see that.”
MPs said there would be a significant parliamentary rebellion on Rosebank, unlike Jackdaw, where they were prepared to accept the argument to allow gas to be extracted for domestic consumption.
Fookes said: “The case was made for Jackdaw to some degree and we remained quite quiet over that. Rosebank, however, is a different issue.”

items.title: Russia’s alleged sabotage campaign in Europe raises fears of escalation
items.summary: From drone incursions to an alleged campaign of assassinations, Russia is feared to be pressing a shadow war.
items.content:
Share Russia’s alleged sabotage campaign in Europe raises fears of escalation on social media
Members of an electronic warfare unit of the German armed forces set up a system for locating enemy radio communications during military exercise on October 28, 2026, near Paluknys, Lithuania [Sean Gallup/Getty Images]
Russia appears to have escalated its shadow war in Europe this year.
European officials have alleged that Russian fighter planes have veered inside Polish, Lithuanian and Estonian airspace, testing reaction times. Suspected Russian drones have been downed over Poland, Finland and the Baltic states.
And Moscow has been accused of bringing trouble to the Black Sea.
In two separate operations in October, Ukraine accused Russia of using aerial and surface drones to sink four cargo ships just outside the territorial waters of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member, in an apparent warning that Ukraine’s grain exports through NATO territorial waters may not be safe for long.
Russia and Belarus have also been accused of trying to destabilise the Baltic states by making their borders appear fluid.
“Masked and most likely armed individuals on the Belarus side of the border escorted and attempted to push groups of illegal migrants into Latvia,” Ieva Cesniece, Latvia’s ambassador to Greece, told Al Jazeera. “Those individuals expressed threats to Latvian soldiers and border guards. On the same day in a separate incident, masked individuals crossed into Latvian territory and carried out deliberate sabotage. Bborder infrastructure was damaged, and surveillance equipment was removed.”
Latvian media have reported that asylum seekers and undocumented migrants who tried to run back from the Latvian border were rounded up by Belarusian authorities and pushed towards Latvia again.
Cesniece drew a direct link between the Russian war in Ukraine and its shadow war in Europe.
“The weaker Russia appears in Ukraine, the more it tests our resilience, trying to weaken NATO and EU resolve and support for Ukraine,” she said.
As European governments warned of an imminent escalation of a Russian shadow war on the continent, experts said the bloc needs to do more to deter Russia as well as defend itself.
“Protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening intelligence services and preventing attacks are essential, but deterrence is about more than preventing the next incident,” said Olena Tregub, cofounder and head of Ukraine’s Independent Anti-Corruption Commission. “It is about convincing your adversary that continuing these operations will become too costly. And I’m not sure Russia currently sees those costs as sufficiently high.”
As an expert on following money trails, she believes European governments have not done enough to identify the networks behind operations, expose the command structures, disrupt their financing and logistics, and impose consequences.
Meanwhile, Russia’s war is going badly on the ground.
Two Ukrainian counteroffensives have blunted Moscow’s main thrust to capture the eastern region of Donetsk and in effect have deprived it of any territorial gains this year.
Since a failed August operation to blow up cargo planes at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport, which was later verified by the European Commission as a Russian operation, warnings of further escalation have multiplied.
Czech spy chief Michal Koudelka warned in September that Russia might attempt a military attack on a NATO member in “months, not years”.
Days later, Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova openly declared that European defence industries supplying Ukraine were legitimate targets for Moscow.
“Russia does not necessarily distinguish between the military capabilities Ukraine uses on the battlefield and the European infrastructure that makes those capabilities possible,” Tregub told Al Jazeera.
“From Moscow’s perspective, a factory producing military equipment for Ukraine, a logistics hub transporting that equipment or a company providing critical technology can all become potential targets of disruption.”
This month, representatives of five EU intelligence agencies told the Financial Times that Russia was seeking to “kill” European defence bosses and target their supply chains.
That followed a report from a German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, that Russia had planted incendiary devices in the offices of defence companies Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing in Munich. It also followed a report on the Politico news site in which EU security officials said Russia was planning to move beyond messaging and claim lives on European soil.
European officials have spoken of strengthening the resilience of their data centres, telecommunications, and other vulnerable networks and industries, but they have not spoken of retaliation.
From the Ukrainian point of view, though, Europe has been slow to see sabotage, manned and unmanned military operations, cyberattacks and information warfare as the early stages of a multidimensional war with Russia, and that failure of perception is itself a weakness.
“Where will he stop if he is currently testing all these drones against European countries, even NATO countries?” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked journalists on October 16, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin. “They are not talking about it very loudly yet. They don’t want escalation, … but you will talk very loudly when there are ballistic and cruise missiles and also thousands of drones.”
“Ukrainians don’t know about any war in Ukraine. They know about war in Europe,” said Oleksandr Danylyuk, a long-serving adviser to the Ukrainian Ministries of Defence and Foreign Affairs and now a Russian warfare expert with the Royal United Services Institute.
Like Zelenskyy and Tregub, he believes the lack of retaliation to its apparent hybrid war encourages Russia.
“Russians are limited right now only by their capabilities because they do whatever they want. There is no reaction,” he said.
He said he believes NATO needs to place more forward troops in the Baltic states to create “deterrence by denial” and to strengthen Ukraine.
Minna Alander, a leading European researcher in security and defence with the Center for European Policy Analysis, said denying Russians travel visas, carrying out retaliatory cyberattacks, further interdicting the Russian oil fleet and sanctioning Chinese suppliers of defence goods to Russia were all realistic retaliations Europe could impose immediately.
Danylyuk said money remains the most potent tool of deterrence.
“The most direct way to punish Russia is to actually increase support to Ukraine,” he told Al Jazeera. “Each time we detect Russian intelligence operations in Europe, we will increase combined support of Ukraine [maybe] 10 percent, 20 percent.”
Yet Ukraine’s allies are signalling the opposite, he observed.
The United States withdrew its military and financial support in January 2025 and recently placed the dependability of its satellite services in doubt . In France and Germany, the governments trail opposition leaders who want to stop aid to Ukraine.
(Al Jazeera) Ukraine has performed better than many expected.
Since 2023, it has designed and built its own weapons and developed its own strategy to halt the Russian advance. It has punished Russia by striking oil installations and weapons factories deep inside its territory.
To reverse the tide of the war and reclaim its occupied territories, it is asking for more money, and it is asking it from the people providing the vast majority of it – Europe.
“Next year, the war will cost 155 billion euros [$170bn]), and we need at least 70 billion euros [$80bn] more from you,” Zelenskyy told the European Council on October 16.
“We could double or even triple the production of drones,” he said. “Just imagine how much more pressure we could put on Russia if we could do two or three times more.”

How will John Healey’s energy support package affect you?
Chancellor’s ‘new course’ includes a £100 one-off payment, low-carbon upgrade loans and an end to standing charges
John Healey has unveiled a package of support for households being buffeted by “global economic storms”.
“I’m setting a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe,” the chancellor said in his maiden budget. In the long term, he hopes that changes in how Britain covers the cost of renewables and grid upgrades will “drive down all aspects of energy bills”.
British households face some of the highest energy charges for three years, with the war in the Middle East driving up oil and gas prices.
Under the government’s price cap, average dual-fuel bills are £1,700 a year and could rise to more than £2,100 a year from January, according to industry forecasts .
So what has the chancellor offered hard-pressed households to help them through the coldest months of the year? And will it be enough to lower gas and electricity bills?
The government’s biggest bet on offering “breathing space” to struggling households this winter is a one-off payment of £100 in January for 20m households in council tax bands A to D. It is also the measure most likely to deliver real benefit for those in need.
The £2.6bn “household energy payment” will go directly into bank accounts to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”, according to Healey.
Martin Lewis, the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com, said households could face a 25% cost increase from January and shouldn’t expect to feel better off than they do today.
Officials are anxious to avoid handing public money to those who can get by without it but they lack household income data to target proposed support. Using council tax bands is “the least worst proxy”, Lewis said.
The payment will be in addition to the Warm Home Discount, which offers about 6m means-tested households in England, Wales and Scotland £150 off winter fuel bills.
A chart showing how poor households could miss out on the £100 energy payment
This measure will offer a modest saving for most British households – but not all, and perhaps not until next winter.
Healey promised to end “unfair and outdated” standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes “in 2027 or as soon as possible after”. This could help almost two-thirds of households to save an average of £45 a year.
A standing charge is a fixed daily fee paid through all household gas bills, regardless of how much is used. It means homes that severely ration their gas use – or use none at all – still shoulder the same cost as a high-income household.
The charge typically adds about £100 a year to bills and the change means these costs will soon be recovered through a higher unit price for gas. For those with below-average gas use, bills should fall. But there won’t be savings for everyone.
Jonny Marshall, an economist at the Resolution Foundation, said households with high gas use might have higher bills when the unit rate increases. These could include low-income households who have bigger families or poorly insulated homes.
A home using 7,000 kilowatt hours of gas a year would save about £40 under the change, but a household using 14,000 kWh of gas a year could be £25 worse off, according to Richard Neudegg, a director at Uswitch.com. A household using the typical 11,500 kWh shouldn’t see any change, he added.
Removing standing charges from gas bills will help two-thirds of households save an average of £45 a year. Photograph: Paul Melling/Alamy
The government has already begun taking aim at taxes and policy costs loaded on to electricity bills that could over time mean removing hundreds of pounds from bills.
This month, it removed the 5% VAT levy on electricity bills for 29m households, effectively saving them about £45 a year.
This was supposed to help households through the coldest months of the year, until March. But Healey has promised to keep VAT off bills until July, extending the annual savings to £50 a year, according to the Treasury.
The move follows a string of cuts to electricity levies over the past year which have shaved about £150 a year off costs.
“For many years, under Conservative governments, policy costs were simply loaded on to household bills through levies,” Healey said. “Today, I am putting an end to that. We’ll introduce a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills.”
Healey confirmed he would consider steps to remove standing charges on electricity too, which ​add about £200 a year to the average ​bill. The savings from this measure remain unclear, depending on which costs would move into general taxation and which would be covered through the unit price for electricity.
Healey will continue to alter a subsidy scheme for the UK’s oldest renewable energy projects, around three-quarters of which has been removed from bills and covered by general taxation. The research charity Nesta said this would lower electricity costs by £42 a year.
Healey has scrapped plans for a levy to support hydrogen projects that would otherwise have added £2.60 to £4.50 a year to the average dual-fuel bill.
The government believes that households could save up to £550 a year on energy bills if they invest in solar panels, home batteries and a heat pump. These savings could rise by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.
To help households access these savings, a Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, will offer government-backed loans of up to £35,000 for low-carbon energy alternatives.
The government said it was committed to rolling out heat pumps through its boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £7,500 to help meet the £13,600 cost of installing one.
Grants of up to £9,000 a year are available to households that are not connected to the gas grid and rely on high-cost heating oil.
For many, the government’s new measures will come too late to help this winter. But there could be support in the spring from a debt relief scheme.
The government said the delayed scheme will “provide targeted support to customers in genuine financial need”. Total household energy debt has tripled from 2021 to a record £5bn and could reach £7bn by the end of the year .
The one-off, targeted intervention has been designed to help those with debts from the 2022-24 energy crisis and little prospect of repaying them.
Nesta has suggested debt relief could be given to about 2m households for a one-off cost of £2.7bn. This would also cut the £29 a year paid by all households to cover the cost of unpaid bills.
More details on the scheme will follow in early 2027, the government said.

Spain begins mourning period after deadly train crash
Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims
Spain has begun three days of mourning after a high-speed rail collision – its second this year – killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
The trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling on Wednesday morning in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to the southern region of Andalusia. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda.
Officials said on Wednesday another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition.
‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain
The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s rail network after the transport minister reported an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash.
Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight to find further victims, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes, according to Agence France-Presse.
Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, told reporters on Wednesday that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.
The Civil Guard has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.
A school in the nearby village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, is being used to allow relatives to enquire about their loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who arrived, some of them in tears.
Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said “long and hard hours” were in store because “every person will manage it in their own way”. “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated,” Garcia said.
Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
In January, 46 people were killed and dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”.
The causes of the accident were under investigation, he added. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he said.
Spain in mourning after fatal rail crash, says Spanish prime minister - video
The first victims to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia civil agent, José Manuel Chacón.
The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media said the missing included a former minister for the People’s party and several foreigners who were likely on holiday in the country.
The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.

A woman walks in front of a residential building damaged in a Russian attack during a local ceasefire related to a humanitarian aid mission in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson, southern Ukraine. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP
A woman walks in front of a residential building damaged in a Russian attack during a local ceasefire related to a humanitarian aid mission in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson, southern Ukraine. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP
Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce holding and demining under way to enable humanitarian corridor, Kyiv says
No reported incidents in 30 hours in the occupied Ukrainian city. What we know on day 1,709
A local ceasefire in southern Ukraine was holding for a second day , both sides said on Wednesday, as hopes grew that vital aid would be able to reach stranded residents. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region amid food and medical shortages and reports many people are now starving and eating weeds . The human rights ombudsmen of both Russia and Ukraine said on Wednesday the US-brokered truce – which came into effect early on Tuesday morning – was still holding . “30 hours of the ceasefire in Oleshky have passed without a single incident,” Ukraine’s Dmytro Lubinets said. “No incidents have been recorded in the 30 hours of the ceasefire in Oleshky,” Russia’s Yana Lantratova said in a similarly worded statement. The ceasefire would be guaranteed by “the physical presence of both ombudsmen: Ukrainian and Russian” on the ground, Lubinets’s office said. Route demining was “currently under way”, Lubinets said on social media, describing it as “crucial step toward ensuring the safe delivery of humanitarian aid and enabling civilians who wish to leave the city”.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that since the ceasefire came into force, there had been “no massive attacks” on the regional capital of Kherson , where about 280,000 people lived before Russia’s invasion. “We’re happy even when we have two, three days for these people. You know, some ceasefire is great, you can see them in the streets,” the Ukrainian president told reporters in The Hague. The truce would be a “huge success” if the evacuation of Oleshky’s citizens went ahead as planned, he said.
The timing of the next round of three-way ⁠talks on a settlement of the Ukraine conflict is linked to the conflict in the Middle East, a Kremlin foreign policy aide has said , casting doubt on whether the talks will take place next month as initially proposed. Yuri Ushakov, quoted by Russian news ⁠agencies, said Moscow had not yet proposed a specific date for the talks. “It will ​also depend on the situation ‌on the battlefield and the ‌situation in general. You can see the situation now in the Middle East. It ‌just doesn’t allow us to hold it in the near future. That’s my assumption,” he told journalists on Wednesday. Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he hoped a meeting would take place in Abu Dhabi between 6 and 10 November.
Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s “genius” and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine, reports Dan Sabbagh . The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation. “Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Tass news agency quoted the Russian leader as saying.
The Netherlands will supply Ukraine with €500m ($557m/£418m) ⁠in military support ⁠this ​winter , the Dutch prime minister said. The support ⁠would be used to supply drones and other material to ⁠strengthen Ukraine’s defence, Rob Jetten said ​after meeting Zelenskyy in The Hague. Earlier on ‌Wednesday, the Dutch government announced it would give Kyiv €1.2bn in non-military support in the next three years. Part of the money would be used for funds that supported ⁠Dutch companies willing to invest in the ​rebuilding ​of Ukraine.
Russian authorities have issued permits for ⁠vessels carrying grain for export to leave the Sea of Azov for the first time since 10 July , ⁠when they closed maritime ⁠traffic ​in the area due to Ukrainian drone attacks, Reuters quoted seven industry sources as saying. They said permits to pass ⁠through the Kerch Strait, which links the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, would be issued for the period ⁠to 15 November.
